name: Cranial remolding helmet

card.summary: A custom infant helmet used for skull flattening (plagiocephaly); studies exist but high-quality evidence on benefit beyond natural improvement is described as lacking.
card.aka: Cranial orthosis, plagiocephaly helmet, molding helmet, DOC band
card.note: Made for infants roughly 3 to 18 months old; whether it adds benefit over repositioning and natural improvement is debated in the literature.

quick.overview:
A cranial remolding helmet is a custom-fitted orthosis worn by infants with positional plagiocephaly, a flattened or asymmetric head shape, usually after repositioning has not helped. It is generally used between about 3 and 18 months of age.

The topic is relevant to appearance culture because head shape and facial symmetry are discussed there. Studies compare helmet and no-helmet groups, and Wikipedia describes high-quality evidence as lacking and use as controversial.
quick.mechanism: The helmet is shaped to leave room where the skull is flat and contact where it is prominent, so that rapid infant skull growth fills the space and reduces asymmetry.
quick.risks: Wikipedia associates plagiocephaly with motor and language delays but states that this does not show plagiocephaly causes them. Insurers use measures like cephalic index to authorize helmets, and norms for that index have been questioned.

lead: A cranial remolding helmet, also called a cranial orthosis or banding helmet, is a custom-made helmet that aims to give an infant a rounder, more symmetrical head shape. It treats positional (deformational) plagiocephaly or brachycephaly, in which the skull is flattened on one side or at the back, and is typically used between about 3 and 18 months of age after conservative care such as repositioning has not corrected the shape.[1] Because head shape and symmetry shape how a face and profile look, the device is also mentioned in appearance discussions, although it is a paediatric treatment rather than an adult one.

Positional plagiocephaly became more common after back-sleeping guidance for preventing sudden infant death syndrome, and mild to moderate cases diagnosed before 4 months may respond to repositioning, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Whether helmets improve outcomes beyond natural improvement is debated. Wikipedia says high-quality evidence is lacking and that helmet use for positional cases is controversial.[1] A prospective non-randomized study of 128 infants compared helmet and no-helmet treatment.[2]

Reviews describe the condition as a source of visible disfigurement for children rather than a life-threatening problem [7], and a 2026 systematic review reports that helmet therapy appears to be associated with faster early correction of asymmetry in moderate to severe cases, with differences from conservative care narrowing over time [8].
infobox: About 5 to 6 months for severe cases (Wikipedia)

paras: The helmet is made to an infant's head measurements and worn for much of the day. Severe cases are usually referred for a helmet, and Wikipedia says it works best when started at about 5 to 6 months.[1] Insurers commonly use the cephalic index (head width to length ratio) as one criterion for authorizing a helmet; a 2021 study updated cephalic index norms in a large diverse population because the older 1987 norms came from a small sample of white children.[3]

Plagiocephaly is a diagonal asymmetry of the head, often a flattening on one side at the back, frequently with some facial asymmetry, and brachycephaly is a broadly flattened back of the head. Wikipedia divides plagiocephaly into synostotic forms, where one or more skull sutures have fused, and non-synostotic (deformational) forms; the helmet is used for the deformational kind [1]. Mild asymmetry is commonly noticed at birth and may reflect a restrictive intrauterine environment [1].

Wikipedia lists higher rates in twins and multiple births, premature babies, babies in breech or back-to-back positions, and after prolonged labour, and reports that incidence rose substantially after back-sleeping advice to reduce sudden infant death syndrome [1]. A 2008 French review also describes an exponential rise in diagnoses of posterior cranial deformities after the 1992 recommendation [11]. Reported guidance includes supervised tummy time and carrying the infant [1].

The skull of an infant grows quickly, so shape can be influenced by pressure over the first year. The helmet is made from a scan or cast of the infant's head and has an inner shell with relief over flattened regions and light contact over prominent ones. Growth is directed into the relieved areas while the contact areas are held back [1][2]. Wikipedia says helmets are most often recommended for severe cases and work best when started at about 5 to 6 months [1].

After the American Academy of Pediatrics' 1992 recommendation that healthy infants sleep on their backs, diagnoses of non-synostotic occipital plagiocephaly rose sharply [7][11]. The FDA classified cranial orthotic devices as Class II devices requiring premarket notification in 1998, and a 2009 review notes that this and the following rise in treatment cost intensified controversy over management [7]. Insurers now often use cephalic index thresholds to decide authorisation [3].

A 2009 review reported that no prospective randomized trial had compared cranial orthoses with repositioning and physical therapy, yet orthoses are routinely used for persistent severe deformational plagiocephaly [7]. In the 128-infant prospective study, 62 infants wore a helmet and 66 did not [2]. A large prospective report of 4,205 infants with isolated deformational brachycephaly treated with a cranial orthosis from 2013 to 2017 found an 81.4 percent improvement toward the normal cephalic index and better results and shorter treatment in infants who started younger [10]. A retrospective analysis of 141,513 helmeted infants across 21 states found that those with Medicaid were more likely to finish treatment with residual flattening than those with private insurance [9].
A prospective, non-randomized, longitudinal study of 128 infants (62 helmeted, 66 not) examined outcomes of both options, and a companion paper discusses the helmet-or-no-helmet decision.[2][4]
A study of 99 patients treated with helmet therapy used three-dimensional analysis to look at cranial and facial asymmetry, including mid-face prominence and ear position, after treatment.[5]
A 2023 systematic review analyzed conservative treatments, including helmets, for positional plagiocephaly in infants.[6]
No studies found on adult appearance outcomes.

The 2026 systematic review concluded that helmet therapy appears to be associated with faster early correction in moderate-to-severe deformity, while current data do not show clear long-term superiority over conservative management [8].

A 16-year surgical series of 256 infants with sagittal craniosynostosis describes endoscopic-assisted surgery followed by cranial orthotic therapy, an example of helmets used after surgery rather than for positional flattening [12]. A national retrospective analysis of infants referred for helmet therapy between 2014 and 2020 across 21 states stratified outcomes by insurance status [9]. A 2008 review described the management of posterior positional plagiocephaly over the preceding 15 years [11].

Wikipedia reports an association between plagiocephaly and motor and language delays, adding that the link does not mean plagiocephaly causes the delay.[1] Prevention guidance cited there includes supervised tummy time and carrying the infant.[1]
Craniosynostosis, in which sutures close early, is a different condition that looks similar and is managed surgically, sometimes followed by orthotic therapy [1].
Helmets are discussed in appearance-focused circles in connection with head shape and symmetry. The published studies concern infants with positional plagiocephaly.

timeline.event: American Academy of Pediatrics recommends back sleeping; positional plagiocephaly diagnoses rise [7]
FDA classifies cranial orthotic devices as Class II [7]
Farkas and Munro cephalic index norms, later used by insurers, are established.[3]
Studies on helmet versus no helmet for positional plagiocephaly are published.[2][4]
Cephalic index norms are updated in a large, diverse population.[3]
Systematic review of conservative treatments for positional plagiocephaly.[6]

angle.text: The helmet is worn for much of the day during the period of fast infant skull growth so that growth is guided toward the relieved areas. Parents and clinicians use it to improve head symmetry; the target group is infants, not adults.
